summary: This section explains how a member of a company can appoint another person as a proxy to attend and vote at a meeting on their behalf. It details the rules for notices, proxy forms, and how long before a meeting a proxy paper must be deposited. It also sets out penalties if the company fails to state proxy rights in meeting notices or improperly sends out paid proxy invitations.
points: A member who can attend and vote can appoint a proxy, but the proxy cannot speak and can only vote on a poll.
Every meeting notice must clearly state that members can appoint a proxy who does not need to be a member.
Any company rule requiring more than forty-eight hours to deposit proxy papers will be treated as requiring only forty-eight hours.
A company must not issue paid invitations to members to appoint specific people as proxies.
A proxy form must be in writing and signed by the member or their authorised officer.
Members can inspect deposited proxies during business hours by giving proper written notice.
example: Meera Textiles Private Limited is holding a general meeting for its shareholders. Rohit, a shareholder, cannot attend the meeting in person. He decides to appoint his friend Anita to attend and vote on his behalf by filling out a written proxy form. The company sends out its meeting notice, which clearly states that members can appoint a proxy. Rohit deposits his signed proxy paper with the company forty-eight hours before the meeting starts, making his appointment valid under the rules.

terms.meaning: A person appointed by a member to attend and vote at a meeting on their behalf.
A method of voting at a meeting, often involving a count of votes by shares.
A legal entity or corporation, such as a company.

watch: A proxy is allowed to vote on a poll but generally does not have the right to speak at the meeting.
